results.title: Forecasting GPU Performance for Deep Learning Training and Inference
results.content: This drives the key insight for NeuSight: un-like prior work, it does not directly predict the latency of kernels using machine learning; instead, it distills the kernel execution into tiles, uses a machine learning model to predict the utilization of the device per tile, and then determines 4 Forecasting GPU Performance for Deep Learning Training and Inference ASPLOS ’25, March 30–April 3, 2025, Rotterdam, Netherlands. Seonho Lee, Amar Phanishayee, & Divya Mahajan Deep Learning Model PyTorch or TensorFlow Target GPU Features L2 Cache Size, Peak FLOPs, Memory Bandwidth, Memory Size Graph Extractor Per-GPU Kernel Graph Tensor Dimensions & Operator Type Tile Latency Predictor (MLP) Per-GPU Kernel Graph Predicted Latency per Kernel Scheduler & Latency Aggregator End-to-End DNN latency NeuSight Tile Database Tile-sizes obtained from training dataset Per-Tile Latency Per Operator Latency Predictor Distribution Strategy dp, pp, tmp Network Latency Predictor Distributed Graph Network Operators and Types, Tensor Dimensions Distributed Graph Predicted Latency per Network Operator Figure 6. 5 NeuSight Workflow NeuSight forecasts the end-to-end latency of a deep learn-ing model executing on a single GPU or a multi-GPU server in three steps: (1) forecasting the performance of per-kernel execution on the GPU as detailed above, (2) combining these kernel-level estimates based on the dataflow graph of the DNN to determine the per-GPU latency, and (3) estimating collectives and network operations and integrating them with the per-device execution latency to determine the per-formance on a GPU server executing distributed training or inference. A.2 Artifact check-list (meta-information) • Algorithm: ML-based GPU execution time predictor • Program: Python, PyTorch • Model: Transformer models from HuggingFace • Data set: Measured latencies of single kernels and end-to-end ML model executions collected from 8 NVIDIA GPUs and 3 AMD GPUs (available in the GitHub repository) • Run-time environment: – Ubuntu 20.04, Python 3.9, PyTorch 2.1.0 or similar – (If collecting datasets from scratch) PyTorch 2.1 + CUDA 12.1 and PyTorch 2.4 + RoCM 6.1 • Hardware: – Any GPU supporting PyTorch 2.1 or similar – (If collecting datasets from scratch) P4, P100, V100, T4, A100, L4, H100, MI100, MI200, and MI250 • Execution: (If collecting datasets from scratch) Sole GPU usage recommended for profiling • Metrics: Predicted latency and prediction error • Output: CSV-formatted predicted latency and prediction error values used for tables and figures in the Evaluation section (Section 6) • Disk space required: ~50 GB • Time to prepare workflow: ~1 hour • Time to complete experiments: ~1 hour using the pro-vided dataset; ~10 hours to collect datasets, labels, and traces from scratch • Publicly available: Yes A.3 Description A.3.1 How to access.

results.title: Hardware Accelerated Inference on Edge Devices at Samsara
results.content: On the Samsara machine learning and computer vision team, we build models and develop algorithms that help our customers improve the safety, efficiency, and sustainability of their operations. Thus, in addition to guaranteeing model accuracy, our team must also ensure that our models run within the stricter compute, memory, and latency bounds afforded by our edge hardware platforms. Notably, many network layers (i.e. graph operations) are not supported by every deployment environment. Other layers, while supported, may not have corresponding hardware-accelerated implementations and thus force a subgraph to run on the CPU (consuming additional memory bandwidth and creating a CPU bottleneck). Graph surgery based helps in this regard, by excising and stitching operations in a neural net computation graph to replace an incompatible operation with a set of supported ones (look ma, I’m a neurosurgeon!). However, in the Tensorflow backend, this Keras layer is implemented as a *tf.reduce\_mean* op, which is not supported by some of the aforementioned execution engines and not hardware-accelerated by others. We can leverage the proto representation of the graph to excise the subgraph corresponding to the offending op and replace that subgraph with another single-input, single-output subgraph that has the same mathematical semantics but with different ops. * b) It looks like tflite supports average pooling (most frameworks should since it’s a very common CNN layer), so we can replace the reduce\_mean with an average\_pooling2d op having the same kernel size as the input (with no additional padding). Once we’ve completed the (sometimes arduous) task of exporting our trained model checkpoints to a platform-supported serialized graph representation and verified that the layers of the converted model are executed with hardware acceleration, we need to benchmark the model and compare the results with the latency requirements of the task. For quantization, we’ve found that certain model architectures or variants suffer less accuracy drift than others and that the insertion of quantization nodes at training time helps ensure that post-training quantization induces less additional error on our validation set. At this point, we’ve picked a hardware platform for our product, trained a model that is sufficiently accurate for our product needs, converted our model, and slimmed it down to run within the latency envelope afforded by our embedded code.

results.title: Profiling GPT2 Inference Latency (FP32) - Math, Numerics, and Software
results.content: I ask the question here: does a large GPT-2 model inference fully utilize the hardware capabilities of an Nvidia A100? Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-2 have generated significant activity in optimizing machine learning inference along two major axes: cost of inference (largely driven by hardware or cloud cost), and latency of inference. At small batch sizes a typical *convolutional* neural networks tend to underutilize compute capabilities of high-end GPUs but still benefit in latency from high memory bandwidth. The reason are small kernels with low occupancy can bottleneck the critical path resulting in bursts of compute intensity followed by low intensity (i.e. underutilization) for example the trace below shows the stream of kernels (zoomed out a bit too far to read which kernels they are) and some high-level performance metrics such as occupancy,compute and memory throughput. We can’t answer this in a vacuum and need to know about the application, but for small batch inference of convolutional neural networks very high-end GPUs do not deliver much extra value compared to their substantially increased cost. Next, using nsight compute and nsight systems I traced and profile the nvidia TRT engines to see what kernels were taking the most time and also to see “overall” how well the engine used the underlying hardware. I conclude from this that while the compute throughput is indeed much higher than what a convolutional neural network would deliver, the overriding source of latency benefit from the A100 on this low-batch inference is its high memory bandwidth (approaching 2 TB/s), which it is almost fully utilizing throughout the whole inference. The results above do suggest that GPT2 inference at small batch sizes does indeed make good use of the A100 with some room to improve in compute throughput (perhaps by better tuning the shared memory and/or caching in the attention layers). However since the A100 has excellent memory bandwidth and GPT2 achieves very high sustained memory throughput we see very good performance on the A100, possibly justifying its cost and use (beyond simply the fact that these instances have the most GPU memory and thus fit bigger LLMs).

results.title: What are some graph comparison tools/software? - Quora
results.content: What are some graph comparison tools/software? Graph comparison spans many tasks — exact isomorphism, subgraph matching, approximate similarity, graph edit distance, spectral/embedding comparisons, and visualization-driven differencing. Graph comparison spans many tasks — exact isomorphism, subgraph matching, approximate similarity, graph edit distance, spectral/embedding comparisons, and visualization-driven differencing. + Designed for large network analysis; supports structural comparisons via metrics and custom algorithms; high performance for million-node graphs. + Widely available in NetworkX, igraph, graph-tool; efficient for exact and subgraph isomorphism on modest sizes. + Visual and algorithmic tools for comparing graph snapshots, computing similarity metrics, and temporal diffs. * Exact isomorphism on small-to-medium graphs: use VF2 implementations in NetworkX, igraph, or graph-tool. * Match the comparison method to the problem: exact (isomorphism/GED) for correctness on small graphs; embeddings/kernels for scalable approximate similarity; DB/Cypher and visualization tools for applied, persistent datasets and temporal diffs. Basically, you can use the same tool or library that you are using to draw the graphs for comparisons as well. However, if you want a rich look of your graph or your data is too large then you can use Tableau or Power BI tools for the same.
